bib.title: FACTOOL: Factuality Detection in Generative AI. A Tool Augmented Framework for Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Scenarios

question: How can factual errors in long-form LLM output be detected across tasks (QA, code, math, citations) when neither claims nor evidence are given?
hypothesis: Pairing LLM claim extraction and reasoning with task-specific tools (search, Python, Scholar) detects factual errors better than LLM self-checking alone.
contributions: Revisit the task of factuality detection and extend it for auditing generative AI
Connect tool use with factuality detection in a unified framework across domains
Use FacTool to evaluate modern chatbots: GPT-4 best, Vicuna-13B weak outside KB-QA

method.summary: A five-step pipeline: claim extraction (ChatGPT prompts), query generation, tool querying, evidence collection, agreement verification. Tools: Serper Google Search, Python execution, Google Scholar via scholarly. Compared with zero-shot and 3-shot CoT self-check on four hand-built datasets, then used to rank five chatbots.
method.task: factuality detection of LLM responses (KB-QA, code, math, scientific literature)

datasets.name: FactPrompts
datasets.size: 50 responses (23:27), 233 claims (177:56) for KB-QA; 100 responses (10:90), 186 claims (33:153) for sci. lit.
datasets.source: real-world prompts from Quora, TruthfulQA etc., responses by ChatGPT; scientific prompts made self-instruct style across CS, business, law, medicine, physics
datasets.preprocessing: claims extracted by ChatGPT then labelled by the authors

datasets.name: HumanEval
datasets.source: Chen et al. 2021, prompts processed per Chen et al. 2022 (CodeT)
datasets.preprocessing: label from execution against HumanEval tests

datasets.name: GSM-Hard
datasets.preprocessing: response label from target value; claims labelled by the authors

other.version: gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 for experiments; always claim extractor

inference.samples: one run per item; no seeds or repeats stated; code: 3 simulated test inputs and 3 potential solutions per claim (plus the response under test)
inference.prompting: system prompt 'You are a brilliant assistant.'; user prompts in Appendix A; claim extraction few-shot with 2 RoSE examples (KB-QA, math); verification zero-shot CoT for KB-QA; Self-Check baselines zero-shot and 3-shot CoT
inference.retrieval: Google Search via Serper, 2 queries per claim, snippets from answer boxes, knowledge graphs and organic results; number of snippets kept not stated. Scholar: paper title as query via scholarly, first hit.

parameters.math_tolerance: round(x, 7) in the example snippet; snippets are model-generated
parameters.sci_lit_match: exact case-insensitive match for title and year; LLM subset judge for authors

other.note: footnote 8: gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 and gpt-4-0314 often returned invalid JSON, so such samples were rerun; released code uses the 0613 versions

metrics.name: accuracy, recall, precision, F1 at claim and response level
metrics.definition: classification of each claim or response as factual/non-factual against author or execution labels; response non-factual if any claim is

metrics.name: ROUGE-1/2/L, BERTScore
metrics.definition: mean over extracted claims of max similarity to gold ACUs

metrics.name: weighted claim-level accuracy
metrics.definition: 3/6 KB-QA + 1/6 code + 1/6 math + 1/6 scientific claim accuracy

eval.protocol: Single run per cell, no confidence intervals or significance tests; claims labelled collectively by the authors (no agreement figure); Exp-III treats FacTool(GPT-4) as golden evaluator.

prompts.text: You are given a piece of text that includes knowledge claims. A claim is a statement that asserts something as true or false, which can be verified by humans. ... Each claim should be concise (less than 15 words) and self-contained.
prompts.where: Appendix A, Fig 6 (full text with two RoSE examples there)

prompts.text: You are a query generator designed to help users verify a given claim using search engines. Your primary task is to generate a Python list of two effective and skeptical search engine queries.

Your task is to write an executable Python snippet that validate the accuracy of the math calculation against the calculated answer. The Python snippet should print 'True' if the calculated answer is correct, and 'False' otherwise.

You are given a piece of text. Your task is to identify whether there are any factual errors within the text. ... The response should be a dictionary with four keys - "reasoning", "factuality", "error", and "correction"

evidence.quote: we often ran into problems where the responses were not valid JSON, requiring us to rerun any samples with invalid response formats

results.claim: On 100 scientific literature reviews (ChatGPT-written), FacTool with GPT-4 reaches response-level F1 94.74 against 21.54 for GPT-4 Self-Check (3-shot CoT).
results.setup: 100 ChatGPT responses to self-instruct-style prompts (10 factual : 90 non-factual); Google Scholar evidence via scholarly; GPT-4-0314 for author-subset judging; authors labelled claims.
results.note: Claim-level F1 95.24 vs 36.71 on 186 claims (33:153). Same response-level number is 94.74 for ChatGPT-powered FacTool too.
results.quote: 95.24 v.s. 36.71 claim-level F1 and 94.74 v.s. 21.54 response-level F1

results.claim: On knowledge-based QA, FacTool with GPT-4 gets response-level F1 71.79 against 57.14 for GPT-4 Self-Check (3-shot).
results.setup: KB-QA; Table 5 does not name the dataset, Table 3 lists FactPrompts 50 responses (23:27) and RoSE 100 responses; ChatGPT responses; Google Search via Serper; claim extraction by ChatGPT.
results.note: Zero-shot Self-Check with GPT-4 gets 65.67 response-level F1 (Table 5), higher than the 3-shot one.
results.quote: 71.79 v.s. 57.14 response-level F1 on KB-based QA

results.claim: With ChatGPT as the query generator and verifier on KB-QA, FacTool is below zero-shot Self-Check at claim level (81.25 vs 84.88 F1).
results.setup: KB-QA; gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 for query generation and agreement verification; tools did not help.
results.note: Response level: FacTool 52.63 vs Self-Check(0) 54.90, Self-Check(3) 48.89. Authors blame reasoning errors in ChatGPT's verification.
results.table: Table 5, row KB-QA ChatGPT FACTOOL, column Claim-Level F1

results.claim: On GSM-Hard, FacTool with GPT-4 gets claim-level F1 98.97 but response-level F1 only 80.36, since it checks arithmetic and not the reasoning.
results.setup: 100 GSM-Hard prompts (47:53 responses, 284 claims 246:38), ChatGPT responses, Python execution of generated snippets; claim = arithmetic operation.
results.note: Self-Check(3) GPT-4 claim F1 95.77, response F1 70.59; FacTool response F1 80.36.
results.table: Table 5, row Math GPT-4 FACTOOL, column Claim-Level F1

results.claim: On code generation (HumanEval, 164 problems) FacTool with GPT-4 gets F1 92.11 against 85.26 for Self-Check (3).
results.setup: HumanEval 164 ChatGPT responses (109:55); 3 simulated test inputs and 3 potential solutions, majority-vote pseudo-golden output; claim level equals response level.
results.table: Table 5, row Code GPT-4 FACTOOL, column Response-Level F1

results.claim: Self-check baselines have low precision on scientific lit review (12.73 vs 100.00 response-level), i.e. they call nearly everything true.
results.setup: 100 reviews, 90 non-factual; GPT-4 Self-Check (3) vs FacTool GPT-4.
results.quote: 12.73 v.s. 100.00 response-level precision on scientific literature review

results.claim: With GPT-4 as the evaluator, GPT-4 is the most factual of five chatbots: weighted claim-level accuracy 75.60, response-level 43.33.
results.setup: 30 KB-QA + 10 code + 10 math + 10 scientific prompts (60 total); FacTool(GPT-4) treated as golden evaluator; weights 3/6,1/6,1/6,1/6.
results.note: Vicuna-13B 50.35 / 21.67; ChatGPT 68.63 / 36.67; Claude-v1 63.95 / 26.67; Bard 61.15 / 33.33. Evaluator error rates were not propagated, so rankings carry the 71.79 response-F1 detector noise on KB-QA.
results.table: Table 6, row GPT-4, column WCL Acc.

results.claim: Claim extraction by ChatGPT closely matches RoSE gold ACUs (ROUGE-1 F1 0.7836, BERTScore F1 0.7174).
results.setup: RoSE 100 reference summaries as text, gold ACUs as claims; mean of best match per extracted claim.
results.note: GPT-4 0.7860 ROUGE-1 F1; FLAN-T5-XXL 0.7326. Similarity to gold ACUs is not a factuality-relevant outcome by itself.
results.table: Table 4, row ChatGPT ROUGE-1, column F1-score

results.claim: FacTool with ChatGPT on math response level: accuracy 78.00, F1 80.00; claim-level F1 98.56.
results.table: Table 5, row Math ChatGPT FACTOOL, column Claim-Level F1

results.claim: Authors list errors: round-off in Python (60444034 / 12 = 5037002.83 judged False), no check of reasoning, limited test-case variety, title and author matching failures.
results.setup: Failure analysis of GPT-4 FacTool, Sec 6.2.3 and Figs 15-18.
results.note: Qualitative; counts of each error type are not given.

limits: Datasets are small: 50 to 164 responses per task, 50 KB-QA responses, and sci. lit. is 90% non-factual; no confidence intervals, so gaps like 71.79 vs 57.14 on 50 responses are unqualified.
Claim and math/KB-QA labels come from the authors, no inter-annotator agreement.
Math checks only arithmetic, not reasoning; response-level F1 falls to 80.36.
Sci. lit. checks only title/authors/year consistency, not whether the cited paper is suitable (footnote 2).
FacTool with ChatGPT is worse than self-check on KB-QA; the verifier must reason over evidence.
Code verification depends on LLM-generated tests and solutions; limited test variety.
Exp-III treats an imperfect detector as golden; only 60 prompts across five chatbots, 30 KB-QA.
Claim extraction always uses ChatGPT, and Exp-I scores only text similarity; results depend on 2023 model versions (0301/0314) and Google/Serper search results that change.

terms.definition: whether the claims made in generated signals (text, code, math) can be supported by evidence under specific rules
factuality at the level of individual claims, defined by a natural-language claim definition
